subject: An AI found the WeChat bug and wrote the worm
bodyMarkdown:
The New York Times reported on Tuesday that a California security firm used its own AI to find a flaw in WeChat and then build a worm that hopped from phone to phone through a call nobody answered. What stayed with me is the cost curve underneath it, because work that used to take an elite team months took a machine a few days.

## What Calif actually built

The firm, Calif, says its AI found a memory corruption bug in WeChat's VoIP stack, the code that handles calls, and disclosed it to Tencent on July 24. The exploit the researchers named WeWorm is **zero-click**, meaning the victim never has to tap, answer or install anything for it to run. Seconds after an incoming call, an attacker could read and send messages, place calls and act as the account owner. The infected phone could then call the next one. Calif says it is the first known zero-click worm that spreads through WeChat calls on both iOS and Android, and warned that at scale attackers could "compromise over a billion phones (or accounts)". Tencent shipped fixes on August 21 in Android 8.0.77 and iOS 8.0.76, and Calif confirmed on August 28 that the server side was blocked too. Nobody found evidence of real attacks.

## One firm's stunt is starting to look like a pattern

In August, a firm called A Security disclosed a Zoom flaw it named ZOOMSDAY, CVE-2026-53413, a zero-click bug in the meeting annotation feature that let anyone in a call run code on another participant's machine. TechRepublic reported that the researchers built a working exploit in under 24 hours using fewer than 20 prompts to publicly available AI models. Zoom posted its bulletins on August 11 and fixed the flaw in clients 7.1.5 and 7.0.6. Earlier, on May 11, Google's Threat Intelligence Group said a cybercrime group had used AI to build a zero-day for a planned mass exploitation event, which Google says it disrupted first. And CNBC reported on September 3 that OpenAI began rolling out GPT-6 Astra, the first model the company rates Critical for cyber capability under its own Preparedness Framework.

## The economics run the wrong way

Finding a bug and writing an exploit was the expensive half of an attack, and that half is getting cheap while patching stays exactly as slow as it always was. Tencent took about four weeks from disclosure to a shipped fix, and Tencent has more engineers than most countries have security staff. A dental clinic in Markham running a five year old booking system does not patch in four weeks. So the window between when a flaw exists and when it closes becomes the whole contest, and cheap exploit generation widens it. The hopeful reading is that defenders get the same tools, and Calif and A Security are the proof, since both found their bugs before anyone else did. The bleak reading is that an attacker only has to be right once, and can now afford to try constantly.

## The takeaway

Update WeChat and Zoom today if you have not, because the fixes are out and the technical details are now public, which is the window attackers actually use. If you are responsible for software at work, find out how many days your slowest patch takes and treat that number as your real exposure. I would watch security budgets over the next two quarters, since the argument for spending has moved from warning to demonstration. And watch whether anyone moves to regulate access to Critical level cyber capability now that a lab has shipped one.
